verdict.tagline: Stunning cinematic choices carry the journey, even when performance stutters.
for_you_if: you want a branching narrative shaped by your choices
you enjoy interactive cinematic stories over traditional action
you appreciate high visual fidelity and motion capture
not_for_you_if: you dislike heavy reliance on quick-time events
you need stable performance without technical hiccups
you want to skip previously viewed cutscenes

citations.review_text: It said online that this game is rather short to do a play through, but if you can get the game on sale I'd 100% say go for it. so far i'd say its like those telltale story games in terms of branching story but with choices that feel like they matter and more of a interactive "movie" experience. In the 1st 1 hour and 30 minutes I'd say there was already a couple of scenes and moments that were worth the "movie" ticket, had me wide eyed and another teary eyed, and again only like an hour or so in.

Yes, it is visually striking, and it maybe has an interesting story (btw reminds me of "Better than us" TV show), but that is about it. You can hardly call it a game... I only played for little more than one hour, and I apologize if game becomes radically better later on (but it's not likely from my experience). So, the first scene in game is pretty much a tutorial and showcase of game mechanics. At first glance it looks great and I started to explore the "crime scene" that provides lot of details and insight into what happened. Few minutes in and I realized that all info that is provided is designed to tell interesting story, and give you different dialog choices rather than requiring any reaction from player, making it essentially an interactive story rather than a game. But still, it looked interesting so far... In second mission you are required to walk from point A to point B, pick up package, walk to point C, that's it... There are few optional details to explore and one interaction with angry protesters (you press button to get up after one person knocks you down). Also, walking is restricted to very small area, so you can't stray 10 meters from the path. Now this was very disappointing, but OK... moving on... Third "mission" puts you in control of house maid - your objectives are to pick up trash and take it outside, collect crap, wash dishes, make up beads, clean toilet, mop the floor.... wtf? room service simulation???? You actually rapidly press buttons in order to scrub floor and plates!?!? And most disappointing part is that whole mission is designed just to reveal cliche dysfunctional relation between father and his daughter. And there is no explanation how family on edge of starvation can afford cutting edge robot... Pathetic all around.... After this I tried playing one more mission, but when I realized that objectives are all about housekeeping duties I just couldn't do it anymore. I'm NOT playing butler simulator, no sir... The end... Maybe I'll gi…

Finished it over a weekend. It's not really a game, more like an interactive movie. Mostly walking and quick time events. Play with controller, keyboard and mouse is bad.

Three androids, three stories. The detective one is the best by far. Hank and Connor are the best characters here, every scene with them is good. Kara story is just sad. Doesn't matter what you choose, all endings are sad or very sad. Markus is cringe. Too preachy, not subtle at all.

Choices actually matter which is rare. People can die for good and story just continues without them. The flowchart after each chapter is a nice touch.

Story has holes if you think about it too much. But acting is great. Worth playing just for Connor.

This game is interesting. Similar to Rise of the Machines and I, Robot conceptually. The QTE for every single detail from climbing a ladder, step by step to opening every door is overused and stupid. claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features high-end visual presentation, specifically highlighting character face models, motion capture, and overall graphical fidelity that holds up well years after release.

citations.review_text:
This game has been such a great experience!

DBH is quite durely the most triple-A-ish of all the "choose your adventure" games out there, and the amazing graphics, specially face models, still hold up impressively well almost 10 years after its release. The voice acting is actually superb and choices are heartfelt and matter A LOT.

Which gives also a huge boost in replayability as well, as many playthroughs are encouraged - and enjoyable! While most of gameplay is QTEs and exploration with mild interaction, the writing is superb and themes approached feel even more present now than when the game first released.

Would totally recommend, give it a try!

After finishing Dispatch and enjoying it far more than I ever expected, I started looking for other narrative driven games. That's when I stumbled across "Detroit: Become Human", a game that somehow gets sold for just a few bucks during almost every sale. Looking back, I genuinely cannot understand how a game of this quality is sold so cheaply. It is nothing short of a masterpiece.

I honestly wish I had played it years ago...

This is one of those games that stays with you long after the credits roll. The story is incredibly well written and every choice feels meaningful. I often made decisions that felt right in the moment, only to realize chapters later just how much they had changed the course of the story. It never felt like I was simply watching events unfold, instead, it felt like I was truly responsible for them and that made every success, every mistake and every sacrifice hit so much harder.

The characters are fantastic! They all have their own personalities, motivations and struggles and I ended up caring about every single one of them. Each of the three protagonists is memorable in their own way and I found myself equally invested in all of their stories. The presentation is also outstanding, especially the graphics still look amazing, the motion capture and voice acting are some of the best I've ever seen and the soundtrack fits every scene perfectly. What impressed me the most was the replay value.... seeing the flowchart after each chapter and realizing how many different paths and endings existed immediately made me want to start another playthrough.

The game is an emotional, thought provoking experience that constantly makes you reflect on what it means to be human. It is easily one of the best narrative games I have ever played and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys story driven games. If you've been skipping this game because it looks old or because it's always on sale for the price of a coffee, don't make the same mistake I did. Some gam…

After finally getting to play this masterpiece of a game years after launch, I can still firmly say that it continues to hold up till this day. From the writing to the mocap and all of the way to the ambient music which helps paint a narrative I can confidently say, within my 24 hours of playing, I enjoyed every minute of it.

Graphics, facial animations and world details are astounding, even so many years after release. The only thing that annoys while playing are the unnecessary quicktime inputs while doing mundane actions.

Detroit: Become Human is one of the best narrative driven games I’ve played and an easy recommendation for anyone who enjoys story focused experiences.

The performance was excellent throughout my playthrough, and the visuals are absolutely stunning. Even years after its release, the character models, facial animations, and environments still look incredible.

The story kept me invested from beginning to end. The choices feel meaningful, and seeing how different decisions shape the narrative makes every playthrough feel unique. It’s one of the few games where I genuinely wanted to see what would happen if I made different choices.

The characters are another major highlight. They’re well written, memorable, and easy to become attached to. Each protagonist has their own compelling journey, and I found myself equally invested in all of them.

The gameplay isn’t mechanically complex, but it doesn’t need to be. It serves the story well and keeps you engaged without slowing the pacing.

if you enjoy exceptional storytelling, memorable characters, meaningful choices, and some of the best visuals in the genre, Detroit: Become Human is absolutely worth playing.

claims.claim: Players experience frustration with the inability to skip previously viewed cutscenes and dialogue during subsequent playthroughs.

citations.review_text: I bought Detroit: Become Human for the sci-fi, cyberpunk setting, not because I'm a huge fan of cinematic interactive movies. In fact, this genre really isn't my thing. But credit where it's due: the story is engaging, the acting is excellent, the soundtrack fits perfectly, and the world is immersive enough to keep you wondering what would happen if Androids really started asking awkward questions like, "Do I have rights?" Calling it a game, though, is a bit generous. Most of the time you're watching beautifully directed cutscenes, occasionally interrupted by a quick-time event reminding you that your controller hasn't disconnected. There aren't really puzzles to solve or much gameplay to master. I kept thinking of L.A. Noire, which struck a much better balance between storytelling and actually letting you play. Still, the branching story is impressive, but it also exposes some cracks. If you explore enough paths, you'll eventually stumble across the occasional bug. (At one point Simon very dramatically sacrificed himself... only to casually show up again near the end. Apparently death is just a software update.) And here's my biggest complaint: why on Earth can't you skip dialogue you've already watched on a second playthrough? This genre practically begs you to replay it to explore different choices, yet the game insists you sit through the same conversations over and over again. That's not emotional storytelling, that's emotional endurance. Will I go for 100% achievements? Nope. I know it's possible in two playthroughs with a guide, but following a guide in a choice-driven game feels like asking someone else to make your decisions. Kind of defeats the whole point. A solid 7/10 on my book.

pros:
- Richly story-driven with compelling characters and acting
- moving, beautiful, exciting
- especially relevant now in the age of AI
- intriguing to consider the paths not taken, great if you love a 'choose your own adventure' style
- elegant contextual typographic button cues if you're into graphic design
- lots of replay value to try out different branching paths


cons:
- large portions are on rails and in those, the button pressing is to give you something to do while the director makes you sit still and listen to the story, This is an interactive movie more than a game.
- gets in its own way with frustrating viewing angles, sacrifices UX for cinematic shots which disorientate you and stop you being able to see where you're going
- you're often staring at the button cues so you don’t actually see the action on screen, and the cues sometimes even obscure action temporarily
- replay can get tedious because you can't skip past the on-rails parts and have to sit through them over and over

Overall I think it's worth playing, it's innovative and moving and worth a punt - as long as you accept that it's not a normal game where you have free rein over everything.

This game had me immersed from the second I started, I basically didn’t put it down. Runs really well on Steam Deck too, which made it easy to just keep going.

What got me most was how connected I felt to the characters. When I messed up, it took everything not to go back and fix it. But playing it all the way through and actually accepting the consequences ended up being the best way to experience it - mistakes and all.

It was fun going back and learning different storylines, but sitting through some of the same cutscenes over and over again was a little tedious if you’re just trying to figure out what other scenes are out there - other than that it was a really well done story.

Still works though, albiet with some visual artifacts (blue rain blobs cough cough) and occasional infrequent crashes during scene transitions.

Great game if you love games that respect your decisions. For those who do not like QTE's, this game is not for you as there are many. But if you can get past that part, the game has a good story with some cool investigations and many, many branching pathways to get to varied different endings. Lots of replayability to see all the different paths the main characters could have taken. Overall, solid game!

[h3] "An eye for an eye and the world goes blind." [/h3]

Detroit: Become Human is an interesting game. I played Heavy Rain and Beyond Two Souls when I was a kid, enjoyed them a fair amount. I think it's fair to say that I was excited as a 15 year old when DBH was announced. I even vividly remember playing the Demo of the Connor Hostage situation on my PS4 back when it first released-- I tried to do every possible ending, it was great!

Now, revisiting this game after roughly 8 years have passed and I gotta say... this game has aged fairly well. Lots of issues that the game has criticised back in the day such as global warming, artificial intelligence taking over... anything and so on. I want to structure this review in several little segments, where I go in-depth of every aspect that I find worthy to talk about.

FIrst of all, this is a game, yes, but it's a story foremost. The gameplay, like in all quantic dream games is secondary. I'm aware a lot of people love to cry about this and call these games movies and they would be right, sort of. I don't see the point in arguing about whether or not this is a game or not ridicolous and very much pointless. Any person who values art would have broadened their horizon far beyond the classic "fun = good game". If you can't look farther than that then this game is not for you. I personally thought this game was fun even though it had little gameplay. Making decisions, hitting and missing QTE's was a fun experience and was most of the time something you needed to pay attention to or you could possibly lose a character.

The technical aspect of the game is still something I'm surprised about. I know this is a port-- but this is a PlayStation port. There are not many PS ports that I can mention personally that function at all. (TLOU1 & 2, looking at you...). I've not had any issues with this game at all whether it's stuttering or crashes except for ONE singular time right before the end at a checkpoint. I didn't lose any progr…

DBH lets the player experience its near-future world, set in the 2038 Detroit, by experiencing the story of 3 protagonists by the name of Connor, Markus and Kara. All of them are androids who find themselves in a world in crisis: with unemployment on the rise the attitude to androids is more skeptical and hostile than ever, all the while humans depend on them more and more. 

This is probably the best entry in the genre of games that could be labeled "telltale-like / interactive narrative CYOA"-game (at least to my knowledge). This game is build SO LATERALLY (i.e.: there are so many outbranching possible alternative storylines depending on the choices by the player), that some story paths have a statistically insignificant amount of players, resulting in a rounded down 0% within the in-game statistics. As you play the characters, their fate is directly influenced by the decisions you make for them (and your ability to succeed in QTEs every so often). There are real chances of losing your protagonists prematurely by acting poorly, upping the stakes quite a bit.

Quantic Dreams dedication towards actually exploring all these routes to begin with, story-writing them, motion-capturing them, etc. for the sake of making a truly interactive and immersive experience is [u] honestly applaudable. [/u]

The music of DBH is also really enjoyable, creating suspense when needed, or delivering a more gentle and emotional assamble of strings when something sad happens on screen. David Cage's vision for the game was it also for each character to "feel" different. Therefore camera-angles/cinematography is different between characters and each character's OST was written by a different composer. From the emotional strings of Philip Sheppard for Kara to the cold, calculated and electrical sounds of Nima Fakhrara for Connor, they also help in setting the scene tremendously.

The game also makes it really easy for the player to explore its world; at any point the player can select a prev…

citations.review_text:
DBH is one of my favorite (given that this is one of the only of it's genre i've played) story driven games. This is not my typical game as I like strategy based games. Despite the clash of interest in games, I really enjoyed it. One of my favorite parts of the game is the minor details and gameplay mechanics that puts you into the body of an android. You as the player feel for these androids and are embodied in their daily lives.

One more thing I would like to address is the modern themes baked into this game. There are a few themes like the holocaust, slavery, and AI advancement. I will not discuss further about the first two as it is a very polarizing topic and I do not want to put anything forward, so I will solely talk about AI advancement. I think this game was ahead of it's time. The themes, issues, and dilemma faced by you the character as well as other people in the game are real things we have to question about and solve for. Especially in a modern era where AI advancement has became so much more apparent, everything that happens feels realistic. It is funny to joke about the future, but this realism has only became more true as time goes on. Am I exaggerating all of these claims? Well possibly, but even so, that's how good this game is. It takes you to take another perspective from 1: androids and 2: the human civilization. 

Overall 9/10. One issue I have with this game is the camera as the perspective is very annoying and bugs out some times.

(My mistake) was not knowing how to interact with stuff as I (for some stupid reason) did not know you had to hold your LMB when interacting.

Unique game with great branching storyline. I really enjoyed it. Camera is difficult to control sometimes, and game will crash on occasion, but I highly recommend this game for people looking for a story driven narrative with real choices and consequences.

This is the first choices-matter game that I've played ever, and [b] Detroit: Become Human completely blew my expectations on what I thought this game was about. [/b] First though, we have to get into one of the only negative parts about this game, and it relates to the PC side of Detroit: Become Human.

I'm not sure why, but for some odd reason the game sometimes likes to crash on me multiple times whenever I'm playing. It's not just me, though. This has happened to other people as well who play on a PC when playing Detroit: Become Human. Thankfully, it only crashes on me during the start of cutscenes when my game saves and not during important moments, but I don't think I can say the same for other people who have played Detroit: Become Human. The error tells me that I need to update my drivers, but when I searched more in-depth about this issue I saw other people updating their drivers and the issue still popping up whenever they play, so I decided to skip the task of updating my driver and continue playing. That's probably the only negative part about this game, so now I'll be going into why I love this game.

Firstly, the story is amazing. Not only do you have three seperate stories for three seperate characters, but each of them are very interesting. I won't be getting into the specifics just so that you won't be spoiled, but in my personal opinion I really love watching the story for all of these three characters unfold into something that I would never imagine it to be. It's something that I have almost never seen in my entire life, and the fact that there are three seperate ones makes it even better, with all due honesty. 

Secondly, the replay value is out of this world. Currently, as I'm writing this review, I have played the entire game two times. I am certain that each of those two times that I have played I have definitely enjoyed all the way through.
